summary: T1, T3, T4, T5 verified fixed by executing the named mutations. T2 is NOT fixed: the eagerness of the over-long check remains entirely unconstrained. Reds are honest -- all 8 new tests carry red records bound to the final test-source hash 7fc7ad44, and red.log shows genuine assertion/IOException failures at the right line numbers, not compile errors.

findings.title: T2 is not fixed: no test distinguishes the eager check from a lazy one, because readAllBytes reaches EOF
findings.failure_scenario: checkedStreamRefusesAnOverLongBody uses in.readAllBytes(), which drives the stream to EOF. At EOF read(byte[],int,int) returns -1 and calls verify(). So a lazy implementation ALSO throws from inside the readAllBytes() call -- the assertThatThrownBy(() -> in.readAllBytes()) wrapper cannot tell where the throw originated. VERIFIED SURVIVING MUTATION, executed: strip the throw from count() so it only does seen += n, and add `if (seen > length) throw new IOException("body declared " + length + " bytes but yielded more (" + seen + ")");` to the top of verify(). This is exactly the pre-fix lazy design with the new wording. All 17 tests pass (tests=17 failures=0, ./gradlew :binstore-spi:test --rerun-tasks). The comment on line 115 claims 'the throw must come from the READ, not from close()' -- true under both designs, so it constrains nothing. Consequence: the whole reason the eager check exists (stop the backend before it commits the S3 request) can be deleted and the suite stays green. FIX, verified to kill the mutant: a consumer that over-reads WITHOUT reaching EOF. Body(2, "much longer"), then assertThatThrownBy(() -> in.read(new byte[5], 0, 5)) -- the delegate has 11 bytes so read returns 5 and never sees EOF; eager throws, lazy returns 5 silently. Confirmed: added it, passes on HEAD, fails on the mutant (failures=1, probeEagerRefusalBeforeEof).

findings.title: The eager-refusal path never closes the stream, so close()-after-eager-refusal is untested
findings.failure_scenario: checkedStreamRefusesAnOverLongBody obtains the stream outside try-with-resources and never closes it -- the one new test that leaks its delegate, in a commit whose T4 finding was about delegate leaks. Nothing covers the ordinary caller shape (try-with-resources around a body that is refused mid-read). VERIFIED SURVIVING MUTATION, executed: delete `verified = true;` from count(). All 17 tests pass. Under that mutant a try-with-resources caller gets a second IOException from close() suppressed onto the first, and `verified` as a latch is unconstrained.

findings.title: The mark() no-op override is asserted by a comment, not by an assertion
findings.failure_scenario: The test comment says 'mark() must be a no-op too', but reset() throws unconditionally regardless of whether mark() was called, so nothing observable distinguishes the override from a forwarding call. VERIFIED SURVIVING MUTATION, executed: replace the empty body of mark(int) with `super.mark(readlimit);`. All 17 tests pass. This is arguably an equivalent mutant at the API surface -- the point is that the production javadoc on mark() states a rationale the suite cannot check, so it should be recorded as disclosed-equivalent alongside the !sawEof one rather than left reading as tested behaviour.
